projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Sigmund Louis Lieberman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Good afternoon. Today is May 28, 2010. My name is Michelle Geren. I am conducting an oral history interview at the Court Reporting Institute of Dallas in Dallas, Texas, with Sig Liberman.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Please state your name and address for the record.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Sigmund Liberman, 440 Independence Parkway, Plano, Texas 75075.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Seattle, Washington.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: And why did you join?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Why did I join?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: I wanted to become an air force navy officer, but I was color blind so they refused me and I joined the army.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: First date?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: First days in service.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, they sent me to Fort Lewis Washington and I was going to go to Transportation Corps OCS, but they kept me there and kept me there and kept me there for over a month, and then they finally needed some infantry people so they sent to me to Weatherford, Texas.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: My instructors? No, not there.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Okay. Tell me about your boot camp training experiences.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, boot camp was pretty warm in Texas at the time, and I remember a few instances where we had forced marches and the instructors would always tell us to put salt in our water so we wouldn't be drinking so much. And we did that and then he would come along and put extra salt in there, so it was like being in the ocean. And so we did not drink much water at the camp.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Which wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Which war?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Which war or wars.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Word War II, and I was called up for Korea but did not serve.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: From Fort Lewis I went to Camp Wolters Texas at Weatherford, Texas, and then I was taken out of there to go to Army Engineer ASTP, and I went to Florida University for a year.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What was your job or assignment?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, at that time I was training to be an engineering officer, but they needed some more infantry in Europe so they took us all out of ASTP programs and sent us all to infantry.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did you see combat?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes, quite a bit. I received a Combat Infantry Badge which means I was on the front lines for over a hundred days.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Were there many casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Quite a few. I guess, overall, we had almost 90 percent casualties. We had some people -- some soldiers who would come up in the evening as replacements and they would be dead in the morning, so.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Tell me about a couple of your most memorable experiences.

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, there were two of them. Number one, was I was sent to Nordhausen concentration camp to open up the gates and I was a liberator of Polish and French citizens, and the Jews had already been taken out of there and sent on their way to other concentration camps. They were put in warehouses and burned to death. But at Nordhausen they didn't shoot anybody cause they needed the ammunition, so they starved them. And when we entered the gates there were five thousand stacked up like cordwood and a few living were actually like skeletons walking around. And the other experience I had was being as a Jew. All my men knew I was Jewish and I was a squad leader and reconnaissance sergeant during the war, and we were surrounded by Germans. And so they knew if I was captured I would be shot. So they threw me in -- we were in this warehouse full of sugar turnips and they put me in the middle of the sugar turnips and covered me and a few others up and the Germans came in and the men surrendered. But the Germans did not shoot into the sugar beets; they just poked around with their bayonets and we were too far inside so we walked out of there.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: During all of this, how did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, the only thing I did was whenever I got an opportunity to write a letter, which wasn't very often, maybe once every other week or so, I would write a letter, and, of course, they were writing to me and whenever we got mail, everybody was anxious to get letters. And we had a buddy who was in the service with me who was from Philadelphia, and he knew some girls who wanted pen-pals so I became a pen-pal with one of them.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Food? It wasn't very good. We used a lot of rations, either C-rations, or three-in-one. C-rations are canned and three-in-one is a box with three meals in it, and they were a little better when we could get them. When we were travelling I had a jeep as a motor squad leader, and my jeep driver would always have fresh eggs and cheese or sausage or something, so we always had eggs.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Was there something special you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Was there something special you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: For good luck? Carried a bible.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, I don't know. Most of them smoked and told stories. I didn't smoke at the time, so I was able to ration out the cigarettes to different people. And so I got extra rations which was a D bar which was a solid chocolate square, about 3 inches by 1 inch by 1 inch and a solid chocolate, and I got all of those because nobody else wanted them.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What did you do when you went on leave?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: On leave? I never got a leave except one time I got a three-day pass to Paris, and we went on a 40 and 8 to Paris. We had no money, but we had two cartons of cigarettes which helped us through. And we were going to see, I think it was Harry James, but he didn't arrive. He died when he was flying over to France from England.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you have photographs?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. I have quite a few photographs of my people that served with me. And then I have photographs from the concentration camp that we opened up. And I've given talks on that particular episode of my life. And I returned from Waco last month where I gave a talk on the concentration camp to the (creator) Of Waco religious leaders, and I was invited to go to Baylor University to give the same speech, but I haven't consummated that as yet. I was -- gave a talk to some students at North Texas State and I've given talks to different high schools and grade schools. And one of the highlights of giving this talk, of course, they have all been different, I gave it to a high school -- middle school here in Dallas. And after the talk, a young girl came up to me and said, "Thank you, Mr. Liberman." And I said, "Thank me for what?" She said, "If you hadn't opened up that concentration camp I wouldn't be here." Both her grandparents were in that camp that we had opened up, unbeknownst to me and anybody else.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Did I keep a personal diary? Yes, but I don't have it now.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, my original days ended in 1945 when the war was over and we were sent to Camp Roberts, California, to train for the invasion of Japan. And President Truman let the atomic bomb go off and as a result the war in Japan ended so we were discharged from San Luis Obispo, and I went home and then I received a direct commission from President Truman. And I joined the reserve and national guard and advanced to the rank of major.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did you make any close friendship while in the service?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. At the time I met some close friends. I kept in contact with a couple of our sergeants through our reunion association. And I met my jeep driver who lived in Laredo, Texas, and went down to see him one time and we spent the weekend together.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What did you go and do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: What did you do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: After the war I went back to college to get my degree, and then I got a graduate degree in international relations from AIFT in Glendale, Arizona. I was hired by Sears Roebuck to go to Mexico, but that didn't pan out so I went back to Arizona and went into business with my father-in-law who ran a department store. And we ended up with two department stores, and then finally in 1976 -- no '73 we sold the department stores and I moved to Arizona, I mean to Texas, and became a traveling salesman for LaBaron clothes and western outfits. And so I travelled the western states, as well as the middle Mississippi states as a traveling salesman.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. I enjoyed the military. My wife did not. After I received my commission and we were married, she didn't appreciate it, I did. I felt it was very worthwhile, and I did learn a lot from it and, of course, that's why my kids call me "General" because I always give orders and I gave orders all the time as a sergeant and then as a major and as a second lieutenant on up to major.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did you join a veteran's organization?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. I joined the VFW, the American Legion, the Disabled American Veterans, the Veterans of Foreign Wars, and the Jewish War Veteran, and which I am -- was commander here in Dallas, and I still belong to the JWV as well as the TVA.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you attend reunions?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Do you attend reunions?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. We have a reunion every year. I attended one reunion in San Antonio, which was very nice, and met a few people from our battalion who were there and a couple of people from my company who were there.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: How did your service and experiences affect your life in general?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, I'm one of the veterans of World War II who like to talk about it because today the students in grade school and high school don't know anything about World War II. So I do go around talking to different schools upon invitation, and I've been known to talk an awful lot. But anyway, it has taught me respect of the flag and respect of the country and respect of others and hope that it shall never come again such a war as World War II or the concentration camps. That we never shall see them because it's not worthwhile and it's real bad.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that hasn't been covered in the interview?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Well, the only thing is I would like to make sure that the the younger generation are taught something in history about World War II or even the genocide that occurred because I'm hoping that it never happens again. And yet there's genocide in Dapur, Africa, there's been in Russia, there's been in China, and it's been all over. And it's not a good episode for us to repeat because there's no sense in killing anybody just because they are the opposite sex or the opposite religion. And with the Muslims and the getting a hand on their Jihad I feel that we are in danger and we should know about it and not listen to just what's in the newspaper but actually try to study it. And I hope that the students of today really get down to earth and understand what's going on, and the teachers of today learn a little bit about it and talk about it. And with Memorial Day coming up I think it's very, very important for us to remember all those who are killed in the war as well as those who served.

sp.speaker: Michele Geren
sp.p: Did you receive any awards?

sp.speaker: Sigmund Louis Lieberman
sp.p: Yes. I received a Combat Infantry Badge which I was on the front line over a hundred days. I received a Purple Heart for injuries, the Bronze Star for heroism, and, of course, a Good Conduct Medal, the European Theatre Medal a few of those. But I'm real proud of the Purple Heart and the Bronze Star which is for heroism, and I felt that at one time I should have received a higher honor, but being in the infantry and being a sergeant very few of us got high awards as they all went to the officers during the war. But I'm real proud of it, as you see, I wear my cap. It's a Purple Heart cap with my medals on it. So that's about it.
